content: The MT-ATP8 gene, also referred to as ATP8, is a mitochondrial gene formally named mitochondrially encoded ATP synthase membrane subunit 8. This gene encodes a subunit of the mitochondrial ATP synthase enzyme, specifically the ATP synthase Fo subunit 8, also known as subunit A6L. This subunit is part of the Fo complex, which is a component of the large, transmembrane F-type ATP synthase enzyme. ATP synthase, also called Complex V, is responsible for the final step of oxidative phosphorylation in the electron transport chain. One segment of ATP synthase facilitates the movement of positively charged ions, known as protons, across a specialized membrane within mitochondria. Another segment of the enzyme harnesses the energy generated by this proton flow to convert adenosine diphosphate (ADP) into adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The sequence of subunit 8 varies among metazoans, plants, and fungi. In humans and other mammals, the ATP synthase protein 8 is encoded by the MT-ATP8 gene located in the mitochondrial genome. When the complete human mitochondrial genome was first published, the MT-ATP8 gene was initially described as an unidentified reading frame, URF A6L. A unique feature of the MT-ATP8 gene is its 46-nucleotide overlap with the MT-ATP6 gene. The MT-ATP6 gene begins in the +3 reading frame relative to the +1 reading frame of MT-ATP8. The MT-ATP8 protein has a molecular weight of 8 kDa and consists of 68 amino acids. It is a subunit of the F1Fo ATPase, also known as Complex V, which is composed of 14 nuclear-encoded and 2 mitochondrial-encoded subunits. F-type ATPases are structurally divided into two domains: the F1 domain, which contains the extramembranous catalytic core, and the Fo domain, which contains the membrane proton channel. These domains are connected by a central stalk and a peripheral stalk. As an A subunit, MT-ATP8 is located within the non-catalytic, transmembrane Fo portion of the complex, which forms the proton channel. The catalytic portion of mitochondrial ATP synthase consists of five different subunits (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, and epsilon) assembled in a stoichiometry of three alpha, three beta, and one of each of the other three subunits. The proton channel is composed of three main subunits (a, b, and c). The MT-ATP8 gene encodes the delta subunit of the catalytic core. Alternative splicing of transcripts encoding the same isoform has been identified. The MT-ATP8 gene encodes a subunit of mitochondrial ATP synthase, which is located in the thylakoid membrane and the inner mitochondrial membrane. Mitochondrial ATP synthase catalyzes the synthesis of ATP by utilizing the electrochemical gradient of protons across the inner membrane during oxidative phosphorylation. The Fo region drives the rotation of the F1 domain, which contains a water-soluble component that hydrolyzes ATP. Together, the F1Fo complex creates a pathway for proton movement across the membrane. This protein subunit appears to be an integral component of the stator stalk in yeast mitochondrial F-ATPases. The stator stalk is anchored in the membrane and prevents futile rotation of the ATPase subunits relative to the rotor during coupled ATP synthesis or hydrolysis. This subunit may have a similar function in metazoans. The nomenclature of the enzyme has a long history. The F1 fraction derives its name from Fraction 1, while Fo (written as a subscript o, not zero) is named for its role as the binding fraction for oligomycin, a naturally derived antibiotic that inhibits the Fo unit of ATP synthase. The Fo region of ATP synthase is a proton pore embedded in the mitochondrial membrane. It consists of three main subunits (A, B, and C) and, in humans, six additional subunits: d, e, f, g, MT-ATP6 (or F6), and MT-ATP8 (or A6L). The three-dimensional structure of the E. coli homologue of this subunit has been modeled based on electron microscopy data, forming a transmembrane 4-alpha-helix bundle. Mutations in MT-ATP8 and other genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria have been linked to various neurodegenerative and cardiovascular disorders, including mitochondrial Complex V deficiency, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with stroke-like episodes (MELAS), Leigh syndrome, and NARP syndrome. Most cells in the body contain thousands of mitochondria, each with one or more copies of mitochondrial DNA. The severity of some mitochondrial disorders is associated with the percentage of mitochondria in each cell that carry a specific genetic mutation. Individuals with Leigh syndrome due to an MT-ATP6 gene mutation often have a very high percentage of mitochondria with the mutation (more than 90% to 95%). In contrast, the less severe features of NARP syndrome result from a lower percentage of mitochondria with the mutation, typically 70% to 90%. Because these two conditions arise from the same genetic changes and can occur in different members of a single family, researchers believe they may represent a spectrum of overlapping features rather than two distinct syndromes. Mitochondrial Complex V deficiency presents with heterogeneous clinical manifestations, including neuropathy, ataxia, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy can range from negligible to extreme hypertrophy, minimal to extensive fibrosis and myocyte disarray, absent to severe left ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and distinct septal contours or morphologies with highly variable clinical courses. Mitochondrial Complex V deficiency is characterized by a shortage or loss of function in Complex V of the electron transport chain, leading to a wide variety of signs and symptoms affecting multiple organs and systems, particularly the nervous system and the heart. The disorder can be life-threatening in infancy or early childhood. Affected individuals may experience feeding problems, slow growth, low muscle tone (hypotonia), extreme fatigue (lethargy), and developmental delay. They often develop elevated levels of lactic acid in the blood (lactic acidosis), which can cause nausea, vomiting, weakness, and rapid breathing. High levels of ammonia in the blood (hyperammonemia) can also occur, potentially resulting in abnormal brain function (encephalopathy) and damage to other organs. Ataxia, microcephaly, developmental delay, and intellectual disability have been observed in patients with a frameshift mutation in MT-ATP6. This mutation causes a cytosine insertion at position 8612, resulting in a truncated protein only 36 amino acids long, as well as two T>C single-nucleotide polymorphisms at positions 8610 and 8614, leading to a homopolymeric cytosine stretch. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a common feature of mitochondrial Complex V deficiency, is characterized by thickening (hypertrophy) of the cardiac muscle, which can lead to heart failure. The 8528T>C mutation occurs in the overlapping region of the MT-ATP6 and MT-ATP8 genes and has been described in multiple patients with infantile cardiomyopathy. This mutation alters the initiation codon in MT-ATP6 to threonine and changes tryptophan to arginine at position 55 of MT-ATP8. Individuals with mitochondrial Complex V deficiency may also exhibit a characteristic pattern of facial features, including a high forehead, curved eyebrows, downward-slanting palpebral fissures, a prominent nasal bridge, low-set ears, thin lips, and a small chin (micrognathia). Infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (CMHI) is also caused by mutations affecting distinct genetic loci, including MT-ATP6 and MT-ATP8. This form of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a heart disorder characterized by ventricular hypertrophy, which is usually asymmetric and often involves the interventricular septum. Symptoms include shortness of breath (dyspnea), fainting (syncope), collapse, palpitations, and chest pain, which can be readily provoked by exercise. The disorder exhibits interand intrafamilial variability, ranging from benign to malignant forms with a high risk of cardiac failure and sudden cardiac death.
